account: The 100,000 Genomes Project rare-disease diagnosis pilot appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine, 11 November 2021. It applied Exomiser's phenotype-based prioritization to genomes from 2,183 families in the English National Health Service (NHS). Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders. 92% of the 490 diagnoses came from applied gene panels or Exomiser's top five candidates. Clinicians reported 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses, 25%, were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes, surveillance recommendations, clinical trial eligibility and reproductive planning.

ai_role.statement: Exomiser scored and ranked candidate variants against each proband's phenotype. The pilot reports that diagnoses were detected in 77% of top-ranked candidate variants and that panels and Exomiser's top five were complementary. Clinical confirmation and reporting were performed by NHS diagnostic laboratories and clinicians, not by the software. Neither cited source says who developed Exomiser. The pilot's prioritization analysis was led by Damian Smedley's team at Queen Mary University of London and Genomics England, who are among the paper's authors. An independent evaluation is cited alongside it.

claim_basis: Sources: one independent peer-reviewed study and the deployer's peer-reviewed study. The cited evidence includes no finding by a regulator or court.

comparator.before: A total of 322 (66%) of the 490 diagnoses that were based on SNVs or indels from the genomes were made with the virtual panel–based pipeline
comparator.quote: With the use of phenotype-based prioritization with the Exomiser to score and rank the most likely causative variants, diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates (Fig. 2D). Use of the Exomiser and applied panels was complementary — 92% of the 490 diagnoses were made with the applied panels or the Exomizer top five candidates (last blue bar in Fig. 2D).

fields.account: The 100,000 Genomes Project rare-disease diagnosis pilot appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine, 11 November 2021. It applied Exomiser's phenotype-based prioritization to genomes from 2,183 families in the English National Health Service (NHS). Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders. 92% of the 490 diagnoses came from applied gene panels or Exomiser's top five candidates. Clinicians reported 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses, 25%, were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes, surveillance recommendations, clinical trial eligibility and reproductive planning.
